endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Except with the prior written consent of Customer, Supplier will not disclose, use, license, sell or otherwise transfer all or any part of any Outputs to any third party.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is important to clarify whether the implementer team’s organization monitors and sunsets AI algorithms that are no longer supported and assess whether there is a plan for handling developer-driven EOL processes.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether exit, end-of-life, or change-of-control contract terms reduce disruption when an AI vendor leaves, is acquired, or fails, and no study documents how often that hazard occurs. The recommendation rests on two CHAI framework documents, one of which rates output-transfer limits as a must and the other of which advises end-of-life planning as a should.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the support consists of expert consensus in two framework documents from a single organization.

Both endorsements come from CHAI voluntary frameworks rather than statute or federal rule. One playbook clause bars suppliers from transferring outputs to third parties without customer consent, which may bear on acquisitions. The Assurance Standards Guide asks whether a plan exists for developer-driven end-of-life processes. Neither source specifies sunset notice periods, escrow, or data destruction terms.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures how often vendor exit, acquisition, or insolvency interrupts clinical AI or strands data, and none compares organizations with and without sunset notice, wind-down, data return, or escrow clauses on outcomes such as service continuity, time to replacement, or data recovery. Case series of vendor exits and comparative contract audits would be reasonable first steps.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether safety-net systems, which may have less negotiating power with vendors, can obtain these contract protections remains untested.
